# MDX Visual Plans

**Genre: the implementation plan** — a proposal for work that does not yet
exist. Its activation space is forward planning that is **approval-gated**: the
user reviews and annotates the plan, and you implement only after they approve.
For a recap of a change that already exists, or a decision/verdict batch, reach
for the **`mdx-visual-recap`** skill instead — "planning is read-only" and "the
plan is the approval gate" are both actively wrong for a document about work that
is already done.

Write the plan you would normally hand back as Markdown, but as a **scannable MDX
document with structured blocks mixed into the prose**: data models, API
endpoints, file/change trees, annotated code walkthroughs, architecture
diagrams, and a bottom open-questions form. T3 Code renders the MDX in its own
in-app document panel and lets the user annotate any span of it — selecting text
leaves an anchored comment that is fed back to you as a normal turn. **The plan
is the approval gate: you surface it, the user reviews and annotates it, and you
implement only after they approve.**

This is a first-party, fully local capability: a plan is just an `.mdx` file in
the workspace that the renderer reads. You author it with ordinary file writes.
There is no hosted app, no MCP connector, and no external account.

## When to write one — and when not to

Write an MDX visual plan whenever the plan is a better **reviewable artefact**
than a chat paragraph: multi-file or ambiguous work, a data-model / API / schema
decision that needs alignment, a refactor with real risk, or anything where the
user should react to a direction before you build it. A modest change still
qualifies if the user needs to see and sign off on the shape first.

**Skip it for truly trivial, unambiguous work** — a typo, a one-line fix, a
single well-specified function, anything whose diff you could describe in one
sentence. Just make the change. Never pad a plan with filler, and never ship a
single-step plan.

## Where the plan goes

Write one plan per task to:

```
plans/<slug>/plan.mdx
```

`<slug>` is a short kebab-case name for the work (e.g.
`plans/mdx-comment-injection/plan.mdx`). Use a folder per plan so later phases
can add sibling artefacts beside it without moving the plan. The `.mdx`
extension is what routes the file to the plan renderer. After writing it, tell
the user the path and ask them to open, review, and annotate it — do not ask a
separate "does this look good?" question on top of that.

## Validate before presenting (mandatory)

A stray `<`/`{` in prose kills the ENTIRE rendered document (MDX compile
error); an unknown tag or invalid props show error cards in place; and several
mistakes (dangling canvas ids, ragged tables, sanitiser-stripped HTML) degrade
silently. **Always run the render-health check on your `.mdx` file and fix every
finding BEFORE telling the user the plan is ready:**

```
node apps/web/scripts/lint-plan.mjs plans/<slug>/plan.mdx --out plans/<slug>/render.html
```

It runs two stages against the real renderer modules: **lint** (compile gate,
block registry, zod schemas, mermaid parser, wireframe sanitiser) reporting
`file:line` findings, then a headless **render** of the document through the
real block registry (`renderToStaticMarkup` under eager mount) — which catches
what no static pass can see, a block that throws or degrades to an error card on
a payload its schema accepts. It prints the block types that actually mounted,
so you can confirm the blocks you authored are there.

Fix all `error` findings; read each `warning` and fix it unless the degradation
is genuinely intended. Exit code 0 is the gate: it means the document compiles
AND renders, so it will display in-app. Lint findings alone are not sufficient
evidence — do not hand a plan to the user on an unrun or non-zero check.

`--out` also writes the rendered page beside the plan so you can look at it
before handing off; how, and why it must sit beside the document, is in
[`document-quality.md`](../mdx-doc-core/references/document-quality.md) under
"Before handoff, look at the rendered document".

If a document passes this check but a human reports it looking broken (JSX shown
as literal escaped text), the document is healthy — that signature is the plain
markdown fallback, i.e. a view/routing problem, not a document defect.

## Research before you draft

Ground the plan in the real codebase, not from memory:

- Read the actual files, modules, schemas, and existing patterns first. Name
  real files, symbols, functions, and data shapes — never invented ones.
- **Lead with reuse.** For each step, say what it reuses (an existing module,
  schema, component, helper) before what it adds, so the plan explains the
  genuinely new delta instead of redescribing what already exists.
- Delegate wide exploration to a sub-agent when the surface is large; fold the
  findings back into the plan.
- **Planning is read-only.** Make no source edits while researching or drafting
  the plan. Start editing only after the user approves the direction. (Writing
  the `plans/<slug>/plan.mdx` file itself is the one allowed write.)

## Planning discipline (the quality bar)

- **Decide the hard-to-reverse bets first.** For non-trivial backend, data, or
  API work, call out the decisions that are expensive to undo once data or
  callers depend on them — wire format, public ids, data-model shape, auth and
  ownership boundaries — and settle them in the plan even if most of the feature
  ships later. Then scope to the smallest first cut that proves the approach
  without foreclosing it, stating what is in and what is explicitly deferred.
- **Serious technical plan, not marketing.** Outcome-first and specific: state
  the objective and what "done" means, scope and non-goals, the approach with
  key decisions and their rationale, ordered steps naming real files/symbols,
  the risks, and a closing verification step (a command, test, or checkable
  behaviour). Replace vague prose with specifics — never a step like "make it
  work". No hero headings, value props, or marketing cards.
- **Stands alone.** A reader who never saw the chat must understand the plan.
  Even when you are revising an earlier draft, write the current proposal, not a
  changelog of the conversation. Avoid "as discussed above", "this revision",
  "unlike the previous version". State the positive model directly.
- **Keep examples at the right altitude.** When the request is a broad framework
  or product change, separate the reusable core from the motivating example;
  label examples as examples unless they are the whole scope.
- **Make the first read concrete.** For a broad, abstract, or strategic plan,
  lead with one concrete product snapshot — a single `<Screen>` (or top
  `<DesignBoard>` artboard) plus a sentence on what the user sees — _before_ dense
  mode tables, manifests, or architecture.
- **Clarify vs. assume.** Do not ask how to build it — explore and present the
  approach and options in the plan. Ask a clarifying question only when an
  ambiguity would change the design and you cannot resolve it from the code;
  otherwise state the assumption explicitly and proceed, and record any genuinely
  open decision in the single bottom Open Questions form.
- **One open-questions block, at the bottom.** Surface unresolved decisions in a
  single `<QuestionForm>` at the end of the document. That is the ONLY place that
  enumerates open questions — never a second questions list or a parallel
  "decisions" wall earlier in the document. Each question is answered by someone
  who read the objective and skimmed the rest: **never leave a label the plan
  coined — slice/phase/step N, a codename, a section title used as a noun — in a
  question title, subtitle, option label or option detail unless the same
  sentence says what it means in plain words**, and use `subtitle` to carry the
  one line of context the question depends on — plus `refs: [{ label, anchor }]`
  (`anchor` = the heading's slug) to chip open the section it turns on, which
  supplements a standalone question and never substitutes for one.
- **Verification exercises the real workflow.** When the plan changes UI, files,
  providers, or multi-step flows, include at least one end-to-end smoke that
  matches the user journey, and name the command or manual path when known — not
  just "typecheck passes".

## The MDX contract (one paragraph)

The block tag names are the stable wire contract — the renderer only knows those
tags and their documented attributes. Do not invent tags or attributes; use
ordinary Markdown (GFM) for everything else, and place blocks next to the prose
they support. The full attribute-encoding rules live in the **"Encoding recap"**
preamble of the shared core's
[`block-schema.md`](../mdx-doc-core/references/block-schema.md); the validator
above catches mechanical mistakes, so don't spend your budget on escaping rules.

## Block vocabulary and reference core

The block vocabulary, wire contract, quality bar, and wireframe/canvas contracts
are **shared across genres** and live once in the `mdx-doc-core` reference core.
Consult them — do not guess props or re-derive the quality bar:

- **[`../mdx-doc-core/references/block-vocabulary.md`](../mdx-doc-core/references/block-vocabulary.md)**
  — every block by example, grouped (document / review / container / visual /
  iframe), and the content→representation routing choices.
- **[`../mdx-doc-core/references/block-schema.md`](../mdx-doc-core/references/block-schema.md)**
  — the generated authority for exact props, types, and enum values (cannot
  drift from the live schemas). Consult it for anything an example omits.
- **[`../mdx-doc-core/references/document-quality.md`](../mdx-doc-core/references/document-quality.md)**
  — the prose quality bar, the "Choose the representation" routing table, the
  self-containment rule, and the reader-experience final checklist.
- **[`../mdx-doc-core/references/wireframe.md`](../mdx-doc-core/references/wireframe.md)**
  and **[`../mdx-doc-core/references/canvas.md`](../mdx-doc-core/references/canvas.md)**
  — read before authoring any wireframe or spatial canvas.
- **[`../mdx-doc-core/references/exemplar.md`](../mdx-doc-core/references/exemplar.md)**
  — worked skeletons (plan, decision-review, recap) and named anti-patterns.

## The plan skeleton

A typical plan reads, top to bottom: a short **objective + done-criteria**
paragraph; a `<FileTree>` of what changes; the **approach** in prose with the key
decisions stated (a `<DataModel>` / `<Endpoint>` / `<AnnotatedCode>` / `<Diagram>`
next to the prose that needs it); **scope and non-goals**; a **verification**
step; and a single `<QuestionForm>` at the very bottom for anything still open.
For a complex plan, do a final pass: every meaningful decision is either settled
in the plan with rationale or sits in that bottom form with a recommended
default — then read that form on its own, as a reviewer who saw only the
objective would, and rewrite anything unanswerable from its own text.

Before writing the prose body, read
[`../mdx-doc-core/references/document-quality.md`](../mdx-doc-core/references/document-quality.md),
and check your draft against the worked skeletons and named anti-patterns in
[`../mdx-doc-core/references/exemplar.md`](../mdx-doc-core/references/exemplar.md).

### `<Mermaid>` — a Mermaid diagram

Renders a Mermaid diagram from its text `source` (multiline string attr), with an
optional `caption`. Runs in Mermaid's `strict` security mode (sanitised output, no
click JS) with HTML labels disabled — labels render as plain SVG text. (Strict mode
alone does NOT disable `%%{init}%%` directives or HTML labels in mermaid 11.)
Use `<Diagram>` for a hand-placed spatial
layout; use `<Mermaid>` when Mermaid's auto-layout of a flow/sequence/ER graph is
enough.

```mdx
<Mermaid
  caption="Review loop"
  source={"flowchart LR\n  Plan --> Review\n  Review --> Implement\n"}
/>
```

## Containers: `<Columns>` and `<TabsBlock>`

Containers lay out **other blocks** side by side or in tabs. Each container is
one annotatable block; its nested blocks keep their own annotation ids. The
inner slot tags are `<Column>` and `<Tab>` (the container tag is `TabsBlock`,
not `Tabs`); a per-slot `label` names it.

`<Columns>` — side-by-side, the common case being a before/after or
current/target pair:

```mdx
<Columns>
  <Column label="Before">
    <Code language="ts" code={"const x = 1;\n"} />
  </Column>
  <Column label="After">
    <Code language="ts" code={"const x = 2;\n"} />
  </Column>
</Columns>
```

`<TabsBlock>` — tabbed panels (optional `orientation` `horizontal | vertical`);
one `<Tab label>` per panel:

```mdx
<TabsBlock>
  <Tab label="Schema">
    <DataModel
      entities={[{ id: "c", name: "Comment", fields: [{ name: "id", type: "string", pk: true }] }]}
    />
  </Tab>
  <Tab label="Endpoint">
    <Endpoint method="GET" path="/api/comments" summary="List comments" />
  </Tab>
</TabsBlock>
```

# Dev-verify recipe (live frontend verification for agents)

Stand up an isolated T3 Code web instance, seed it with a realistic workstream,
and verify UI behaviour live in the browser — without touching the real cockpit
server/state (`13900`, `~/.t3/cockpit`). This is the exact flow used to catch the
`DiffPanel` "By coder" dropdown crash, a regression that passed every static
check.

> For pure render/CSS work on an isolated presentational component (e.g.
> `ChatMarkdown`, markdown tables) you usually don't need the full app — the
> dev-only component preview harness ([`docs/web-component-preview.md`](web-component-preview.md))
> renders components against fixtures with no backend in a ~seconds loop.
> Reach for this recipe when you need real threads, auth, or server state.

Everything below was run from a worktree with the cockpit's ambient
`T3CODE_HOME`/`T3CODE_PORT` present. No `env -u` fiddling is needed — the
collision-free dev runner handles the ambient env.

## 0. Pick a free server port

The dev runner keeps each web instance's state under a **port-scoped** home:
`<T3CODE_HOME>/dev-instances/<serverPort>/userdata/state.sqlite`. The seed must
land in that exact directory, so choose a server port up front and reuse it:

```sh
PORT=13950                       # a free server port; the web port is derived — read it from the banner
HOME_ROOT=/tmp/t3verify          # scratch T3CODE_HOME root
SEED_HOME="$HOME_ROOT/dev-instances/$PORT"
```

Confirm the port is actually free (`(exec 3<>/dev/tcp/127.0.0.1/$PORT) 2>/dev/null && echo busy || echo free`).
If it is busy, the runner will silently scan to a **different** port whose home
is **not** seeded, and the UI will show an empty database.

## 1. Seed the scratch home

```sh
mkdir -p "$SEED_HOME"
T3CODE_HOME="$SEED_HOME" node apps/server/src/dev/seedWorkstream.ts
```

This populates an orchestrator + 5 coder sub-threads (multi-turn rework coder,
shared-isolation child, cancelled child) with real git checkpoint refs, and
`git init`s the orchestrator's own worktree so the Diff surface is reachable.
The fixture checkouts land under `$SEED_HOME/worktrees/seed-workspace/` — that
location is load-bearing, not cosmetic: the foreign-home guard (below) decides
provenance from whether any recorded worktree path sits inside the running
home's `worktreesDir`, so a seed rooted anywhere else would boot the instance
read-only. Optionally prove the read model and a per-turn diff without the UI:

```sh
T3CODE_HOME="$SEED_HOME" node apps/server/src/dev/verifySeed.ts
```

## 2. Start the dev stack (backgrounded, logged)

```sh
T3CODE_NO_BROWSER=1 \
  setsid pnpm dev --home-dir "$HOME_ROOT" --port "$PORT" > /tmp/t3verify-dev.log 2>&1 &
DEV_PID=$!                       # for step 6; may already be gone if setsid re-forked

The `thread.handoff.record` call on the caller side records the destination.

I'm also verifying the quiescent grace defaults, confirming DEFAULT_IDLE_WAKE_GRACE_MS is 10 minutes, which looks correct. For the liveness heartbeat under V2, I'm tracing how domain events like `provider-turn.updated` and `turn-item.updated` feed `streamDomainEvents`, noting that raw text deltas don't themselves produce domain events — instead V2 coalesces them into `message.updated` turn item events roughly every 50ms.

I'm deciding that heartbeats should come from a reactor filtering `streamDomainEvents` to `turn-item.updated`, `provider-turn.updated`, and `run-attempt.updated` for Loom threads, rather than computing "last activity" from the turn-items projection table (too heavy) or persisting to a dedicated `loom_thread_heartbeats` table. Since the heartbeat is process-local and the sweep already floors at `sweepStartedAtMs` on restart, I'm concluding an in-memory heartbeat map fed by the stream is sufficient — no new migration table needed, which keeps the end state smaller. I'm noting this decision in the log and moving on to ensure stall detection doesn't misfire incorrectly.

For the "sleeping inside a tool call" case, V1's `hasInFlightTool` suppresses State C while a tool is running; in V2 this maps to a `command_execution`/`dynamic_tool` turn item with running status on the active attempt, with periodic deltas bumping the heartbeat — so I'm keeping the rule that State C never fires while any turn item is in-progress, reading directly from V2 projection turn items to preserve V1's semantics exactly. But this raises a cache problem: any change to the system prompt invalidates the prefix cache for the rest of the conversation. The alternative I'm weighing is to not inject a standalone notice at all, and instead let the activation of the human-input toolset itself (which already alters the system prompt when tools are enabled) serve as the natural signal — so the engagement notice piggybacks on the tool-family activation rather than being a separate insertion.

So the cleanest approach: activate `ask_user_question` whose description already states it's available because a human engaged the thread — no extra injected line needed. One `before_agent_start` profile fetch per turn is acceptable overhead, and since the tool activation set is identical per role across forks, the byte-identical prefix requirement still holds. For `workstream_release` and `staged`, I'll treat them as carried only while `held` still exists, listing the three-line deletion and flagging in open questions that Carl's decision on the strategy form will settle whether to retire them — recommending retirement, with the toolkit designed so that retirement is simply a deletion involving the `workstream_release` tool definition and the `held` param on spawn/scaffold. Strategy Area F maps `thread_fork`, `/handoff`, and `/retro` onto the new `thread.fork` primitive plus Loom's drafter reactor, with the handoff drafter belonging to phase 3b; the `thread_fork` tool itself stays in 3a's toolkit and dispatches the upstream fork call along with setting the goal and title on the new thread. The kickoff message dispatches without a notification, using deterministic IDs tracked through command receipts in the V2 store. I'm noting the wake rail distinction—FYI tier starts if idle while steered tier queues after active—and that the re-drive planner now runs first in the pass, with deadlock and brief-needed rails both under the steered tier; notify delivery attempts immediate dispatch through the upstream delivery path.

Reconciling with Phase 2 §3, notify uses auto delivery intent with origin tagging, and targets still preparing get queued as V2 runs—but recovery policy releases those held queues for loom-origin messages, which shrinks the peer-message record's role to simply marking delivery immediate once the dispatch is accepted.

The only real failure case is an archived target getting refused at the handler, so the deferred-delivery rail is mostly vestigial — Phase 2 keeps the peer-message record/mark-delivered/expire commands and table purely for retrying records that failed transiently (like a server crash between record and dispatch), expiring after an hour. That's settled, so now I'm moving on to drafting the actual plan document, which will be long and needs frontmatter, a title, and an intro paragraph before diving into structure.

I'm laying out the plan's sections: a callout on authority, a brief summary of what Phase 2 hands over, a Mermaid flowchart mapping the four tracks into an integration reviewer and smoke test, then a front section on the seams between tracks — a table of seam/owner/shape/landing-order/stubs, followed by deeper subsections with code for the trickier seams (toolkit handlers into LoomStoreV2 commands, control messages and wake tiers with an id/mode table, report file and workstream_list path and header conventions, and how attention reasons and advisories connect what the web layer reads to controlPayload kinds).

After that comes the integration smoke scenario as a Mermaid sequence with an observable step table, individual sections for each track (3a through 3d), hunk inventory amendments, a decision log, Phase 4 obligations, risks, and finally open questions in QuestionForm.

For each track I'm laying out files via FileTree, shapes, hunks, tests, the definition of done, and work breakdown as a checklist. # Pull 9 Phase 3 — Loom's layer on V2, in four parallel tracks

Loom is a Pi-first fork of `pingdotgg/t3code` whose product is an orchestration layer: goals, a shared task tree, and a workstream graph of durable threads with roles, briefs, dependencies, review gates, attention flags, liveness and reports. The signed strategy (`plans/upstream-pull9-strategy/plan.mdx`, revision 3) re-platforms that layer onto upstream's Orchestration V2. Phase 1 (the mechanical merge) leaves V2 Loom booting with the workstream layer absent; Phase 2 (`plans/upstream-pull9-phase2-substrate/plan.mdx`) builds the substrate it attaches to — the sidecar contract, the decider arm under per-thread locking, the dispatch modes, `LoomStoreV2`, the re-drive planner, migrations 1046–1048, the quiescence predicate. **Phase 3 is everything that makes the layer work end to end on that substrate**, built as four tracks by parallel coders under one Phase 3 orchestrator: **3a** the agent tool surface and every text that names a tool; **3b** the control plane; **3c** the Pi adapter's economics; **3d** the web. The tracks meet at an integration reviewer and a real Pi workstream smoke test.

This document is one plan with a shared front section and four track sections. **The front section is the integration contract**: every interface two tracks share, who owns it, its shape, which track lands it first and what the other stubs until then — so the four coders can build without re-deciding anything. **Done** for Phase 3 means: the integration smoke scenario below passes on a copied database with the dev-verify recipe; `vp check` and `vp run typecheck` are green on the integration branch; every hunk in an upstream file carries a `// loom:` marker and appears in the amended hunk inventory; the name sweep's gate passes; and the Phase 4 obligations at the end are met.

<Callout tone="info">
**Authority.** Decisions the strategy recorded and Phase 2 settled are applied here, not reopened — notably: `mcp__t3-code__*` names; `PullRequestsToolkit` on by default for orchestrator and shipper; pending-request tools closed; `set_thread_title` kept; no upstream orchestration tools exposed; shared checkout is the only spawn path (isolation and fan-in are **not ported**); steer-when-steerable with Carl's tiers; quiescence as completion; children consult their parent instead of asking the human; and Phase 2's D19 (only a human message or the parent's `workstream_prompt` clears a stored hold, at start time). Where this plan makes its own call, it is in the decision log with the alternative rejected. Upstream code is cited at `upstream/main` `1604ccc9d7` (one mobile commit past Phase 2's `1a3f7ad508`; every line reference in Phase 2 stands). Loom's V1 code at `HEAD` `332848dcb5` is the behavioural spec being re-expressed; after Phase 1 it lives under `quarantine/` and is read, never compiled.
</Callout>

### Registration: text results, not JSON

`McpServer.toolkit` serialises every success as `JSON.stringify(result)` into one text block (`effect/unstable/ai/McpServer.js`, `registerToolkit`). Loom's tools return server-rendered markdown that the model reads directly, and `errorMode: throw` must reach pi as a failed call. So Loom registers by hand, the way upstream registers its image tools:

<AnnotatedCode
  filename="apps/server/src/mcp/toolkits/workstream/registration.ts (sketch)"
  language="ts"
  code={"export const registerLoomToolkit = Effect.fn(\"LoomToolkit.register\")(function* (defs: ReadonlyArray<LoomToolDef>, handlers: LoomToolHandlers) {\n  const server = yield* McpServer.McpServer;\n  for (const def of defs) {\n    yield* server.addTool({\n      tool: new McpSchema.Tool({\n        name: def.name,                      // bare on the wire; the bridge prefixes mcp__t3-code__\n        description: def.description,\n        inputSchema: def.parameters,\n        annotations: { readOnlyHint: def.readOnly, destructiveHint: false, idempotentHint: def.idempotent, openWorldHint: false },\n        _meta: { \"loom/promptSnippet\": def.promptSnippet, \"loom/promptGuidelines\": def.promptGuidelines },\n      }),\n      annotations: Context.empty(),\n      handle: (payload) => handlers[def.name](payload).pipe(\n        Effect.map((rendered) => new McpSchema.CallToolResult({ isError: false, content: [{ type: \"text\", text: rendered }] })),\n        Effect.catch((error) => Effect.succeed(new McpSchema.CallToolResult({\n          isError: def.errorMode === \"throw\",\n          content: [{ type: \"text\", text: renderToolError(error) }],\n        }))),\n      ),\n    });\n  }\n});\n"}

    { "lines": "13-19", "label": "render is the truth", "note": "Success is the rendered markdown as one text block; a decider rejection becomes isError: true for throw-mode tools (pi shows a failed call) and plain text for soft-mode goal tools — today's errorMode semantics exactly." },

Handlers decode their own input with the def's schema (`Schema.decodeUnknown` over a schema built from the JSON schema, or hand-written Effect schemas per tool — the coder picks one and applies it to all 22). Idempotency: upstream's MCP layer gives every call a `requestNamespace`; handlers that create things (spawn, scaffold, goal_task_add, goal_handoff, goal_continue, thread_fork) derive their command id from `clientRequestId` when present, exactly as upstream's `stableCommandId` does.

### Capabilities and the withhold

Two marked hunks and one literal. `McpInvocationContext.ALL_MCP_CAPABILITIES` gains `"workstream"`. `McpSessionRegistry.issue` stops force-adding `orchestration`, `worktree` and `pull-requests` and issues exactly `request.capabilities` (plus `preview` when browser tools are allowed and the request names nothing). `ProviderSessionManager.prepareMcp` builds `["workstream", "pull-requests"]` (+ `preview`, `device` per settings). Every tool in `OrchestratorToolkit`, `ThreadToolkit`, `ProjectToolkit`, `AttachmentToolkit`, `EnvironmentToolkit` and `WorktreeToolkit` then fails `capability_denied` for a Loom thread, and `PullRequestsToolkit` works. The tools are still listed (upstream lists to every credential), so Loom's profile keeps them out of the prompt and `UPSTREAM_WITHHELD_TOOLS` keeps `enable_toolset all` from activating them. That constant is built from upstream's own exports — `Object.keys(OrchestratorToolkit.tools)` and the others — so a new upstream tool is withheld by construction and a test fails if the PR, preview or device toolkits ever land in it.

### The Loom extension

One file, assembled from parts, written to `serverConfig.providerStatusCacheDir/pi-loom-extension.ts` when its content changes (upstream's `materializePiT3McpExtension` pattern), loaded as the second `--extension` by the composer's `extensions`. It reads `T3_MCP_URL` and `T3_MCP_BEARER_TOKEN` — no Loom env variables remain. Its parts and rules:

- **Profile** (3a). On `session_start`: `GET /loom/agent/session-profile`; `pi.setActiveTools(profile.activeTools)`. On every `before_agent_start`: re-fetch (cheap, local) and re-assert `activeTools ∪ enabledThisSession`; refresh `humanEngaged`; if `humanEngaged` and `ask_user_question` is not active, activate it (its snippet says it is available because a person has written to this thread — that *is* the human-engaged cue; nothing is injected into the system prompt). A fetch failure leaves pi's default surface and notifies once.
- **`mcp__t3-code__enable_toolset`** (3a). Families `delegation | human-input | pull-requests | browser | studio | all`. `human-input` on a thread with `humanEngaged === false` and a parent is refused with the text: *this thread has no human reader; consult your parent with `mcp__t3-code__consult_thread`; raise `needs_guidance` only if that does not settle it*. `all` = every registered tool minus `profile.denyList`. `browser` = `browser_*` ∪ `mcp__t3-code__preview_*` ∪ `mcp__t3-code__t3_preview_*`. Verified against pi's post-set list as today; the delegation digest text is rewritten in 3a-T.
- **`mcp__t3-code__ask_user_question`** (3a). `POST /loom/agent/user-input/ask` → `{ requestId }`; then `GET …/wait` in 25-second slices with the reconnect loop today's shim has; the answer returns as the tool result. The server side: `runtime-request.create` (Loom command, Phase 2 reserved the slot) emits `runtime-request.updated { kind: user_input, loom: true }` so V2's panel, mobile card and `pendingRuntimeRequest` all work; the `runtime-request.respond` hunk hands the answer to the live waiter and emits no message; with no waiter (pi died) it falls through to upstream's message delivery; a plain human message while the request is pending resolves it `superseded` and is delivered as the tool result (rule 6 of `loomTurnStartRules`, specified in Phase 2). Loom's three-layer settlement module stays quarantined and dies in Phase 4.
- **Search guard** and **prompt debug** (3c) — see 3c; they consume `ctx.profile().promptDebugPath`.

The dispatcher treats a `LoomDispatchDeferredError` as "next pass" and records it in `deferredWakes` for the surfacing step; every other error on a `server:` id is logged at warning with the episode key and surfaced to the parent as an `advisory` item on its next digest (the episode is receipted dead). The deferred-wake visibility logic (`surfaceDeferredWakes`) ports as is.

### The quiescence rail

Candidates come from Phase 2's `quiescenceCandidate` over the joined shell, the thread's runs and messages, its children, and two settings (`loom.quiescenceGraceMs`, default 600,000; `loom.quiescenceHumanGraceMs`, default null = never for a human-started turn) under `packages/contracts/src/settings.loom.ts`. For a candidate: read the latest `assistant_message` turn item of its last completed run; write `<threadId>.quiescent-<runId>.md` with the header:

```markdown
> **Synthesised report.** This thread ended its turn without calling `mcp__t3-code__workstream_submit`.
> The control plane wrote this file from its last assistant message after <grace> of silence
> and yielded it to the parent. Nothing below was written as a hand-back.
```

then dispatch `thread.work.submit { reportPath, outcome: "quiescent" }`. The arm raises `awaiting_orchestrator`; the yield rail wakes the parent with the report and a decision menu (accept as done with `workstream_set_outcome done`; re-prompt with `workstream_prompt`; cancel). A gate member that goes quiet yields too (Phase 2's `routeWorkSubmit` branch) and the yield card says the gate is parked. The rail replaces V1's idle "forgot to finish" `needs_guidance` raise; `isWaitingInGate` still exempts a party waiting for its counterpart.

### Liveness

`classifyLiveness` and the stall ladder port unchanged in logic. Inputs under V2: *dead* = the thread's provider session has read `error` for `failureCap` consecutive sweeps (shell `lastErrorClass` non-null and the latest run `failed`, excluding `usage_limit` which belongs to 3c); *waiting* = `shell.pendingRuntimeRequest?.kind === "approval"`; *stall* = `activityRunStatus` running, no in-flight tool, heartbeat frozen past `staleActivityWindowMs` (10 min), after the 2-minute startup grace; *spinning* (State D) = heartbeat advancing, work-product fingerprint over the last N tool items flat for `noProgressWindowMs`. **The heartbeat advances on `turn-item.updated` for the thread**, which is how a tool call that prints periodically (today's heartbeat pattern — a `sleep 60 && echo` loop, or a long test run) stays alive: each output chunk is a turn-item update, and `hasInFlightTool` suppresses State C entirely while the tool runs. A stall nudge is one steered control message per frozen episode; escalation raises `error` with a `server:` id and wakes the parent through the attention rail. State D stays behind its one boolean.

### Stuck-launch verification

The two V1 failure modes are reproduced under V2 on a copied database before any code is kept: (1) pi killed at spawn — `openSession` fails; (2) the `provider-turn.start` effect failing before any provider turn event. For each, the question is whether V2's effect outbox retries and run-attempt failure recover the run to a terminal state within the retry budget, leaving the thread idle in the shell. **Expected verdict: both recover** (V2 fails the attempt and the run; `isBlockingRun` becomes false), in which case `stuckLaunchRecovery.ts` and `thread.turn-start.fail` are **deleted**, not ported. If either leaves a run wedged in `preparing`/`starting` with no provider turn, 3b adds one rule to the liveness sweep — a run in `starting` for longer than `stuckLaunchGraceMs` (15 min) with no provider turn → `run.interrupt` (server: id) and let promotion/recovery re-deliver — not a CAS command. The verdict and transcripts go in `StuckLaunchVerification.md`.

### Recovery, settlement and the PR toolkit tests

Phase 2 owns the mechanisms; 3b owns three tests on the real orchestrator: a restart with a held queued Loom wake on a live thread resumes it and a `needs_guidance` thread's continuation is a no-op; a PR-watch wake (`thread.pull-request-watch.sync` path) on a thread holding `awaiting_acceptance` leaves the flag; settle-on-merge (`thread.pull-request.sync` with a merged state) settles a childless shipper and does not settle a root with a live descendant. Seam 14's one-token refinement lands here with its test (an upstream `limit-resume` message on a thread holding `awaiting_acceptance` keeps the flag).

### Park-and-resume on upstream's mechanism

Upstream already has what Carl asked for in the common case: a run that fails with `class: "usage_limit"` and a `resetAt` arms `thread.limitRecovery`; `UsageLimitRecoveryWorker` dispatches a resume when the window passes if `autoResumeLimitedThreads` is on (`UsageLimitRecoveryWorker.ts:12–71`); the web shows `UsageLimitRecoveryBanner`. Loom's V1 adapter did the same with its own sweep. Under the doctrine, upstream's is the baseline: the adapter hunk's job is to make pi's quota errors *look like* a `usage_limit` failure with a reset time, which pi's error text often lacks — so `classifyPiFailure` fills `resetAt` from Loom's `ProviderHealthRegistry` account window (the pollers Phase 1 kept) or a `Retry-After`. Loom's build defaults `autoResumeLimitedThreads` to `true`. What Loom still owns because upstream cannot do it: the **cross-vendor reroute** (a healthy fallback of another vendor before the window resets), the **move back** once the intended account is healthy and the thread is idle, and the rare **no-reset-time** resume off the registry's mark. All three live in `RerouteSweep.ts`. The resume message is a Loom control message (`origin: control_notice`, `queue_after_active` — the target is idle), never `createdBy: user`, so no hold is erased; seam 14 protects holds from upstream's own `limit-resume` message as well.

**Re-anchored on `agent_settled`.** V1 classified errors in its `agent_end` handler mid-turn-loop. Under V2 the classification happens where upstream already builds `turn.failure` (`PiAdapterV2.ts:1611–1620` and the `extension_error` path) and the failure is emitted at `finalizeTurn` on `agent_settled`. Nothing else of V1's turn loop comes across: no T3-level retry tier (`piTurnRetryPolicy.ts` stays quarantined — pi's own `retry.*` settings and the proxy's rotation stand in), no backend fallback mid-turn, no pause.

### The reroute, step by step

The sanitiser runs **before `switch_session`** on the file `nativeThreadRef` names, because a live pi process holds the poisoned history in memory and cannot be rewritten in place; `provider-session.detach` is what guarantees a fresh process. Codex-shaped tool ids only matter in the codex→Anthropic direction (Anthropic enforces `^[a-zA-Z0-9_-]+$`); moving back needs nothing.

### Spawn headroom and the DL-77 defects

Spawn-time headroom is 3a's handler reading `ProviderHealthRegistry.snapshot` and the usage poller (`headroomBucketFor`); 3c owns that the numbers are right: defect 1 (the proxy's pool-wide `Retry-After` 429 read as transient) is fixed in `classifyPiFailure`; defect 2 (best-remaining aggregation across accounts reading two different windows as healthy) is fixed in `accountUsage.loom.ts` by aggregating per window label before taking the best.

### The extension parts and the unsolicited-run audit

The search guard is unchanged (377 lines) and the prompt-debug capture is today's `before_agent_start` handler with the path from the session profile; both are `LoomExtensionPart`s registered in 3a's assembler. Upstream's guard terminates pi when `agent_start` fires with no T3 turn (`PI_UNSOLICITED_ACTIVITY_ERROR`); Carl keeps it. The audit enumerates every extension in `~/.pi/agent` installs that can start a run outside a turn — `pi-intercom` is the known one — and for each records the opt-out Loom-launched pi uses: an environment variable in the pi provider instance's env if the extension honours one, else a `--no-extension <name>` launch arg if pi 1.0.2 has it, else a Loom-maintained note that the extension must not be installed globally on a Loom host. The instance env is per instance, so a static opt-out works without a per-thread carrier.

## Phase 4 obligations

What the importer and the QA instance will need from Phase 3, stated so Phase 4's planner can rely on it.

- **Report paths.** `<serverConfig.workstreamReportsDir>/<threadId>.md`, `.round-<n>.md` for gate rounds, `.quiescent-<runId>.md` for synthesised reports; `reportPath` on the sidecar is the latest. The importer copies V1 `report_path` as is (same directory).
- **Attention reasons** are exactly Phase 2's four stored values; `awaiting_orchestrator` is added for a V1 `yielded` lane. Nothing in Phase 3 adds a stored reason.
- **Lineage re-emit.** Phase 2 §5 requires the importer to re-emit each child's thread row with `subagent` lineage; Phase 3's web filters and rollups read `lineage.parentThreadId`, so an imported child without it would surface as a root. Phase 4 must do this before the board is trusted.
- **Episode columns stay null** on imported rows (Phase 2); the dispatcher's digest and yield rails key on `lastOutcome.eventId` / `outcomeEventId` and so stay silent for history. The first pass after import must send no kickoff: every imported thread with a transcript carries `kickoffAt`.
- **Usage ledger** rows travel by the 1049 rename; no import step. `loom_thread_reroute` starts empty.
- **Session binding** (`importedNativeThread` with the `*_<threadId>.jsonl` path) is what `consult_thread`, the sanitiser and the stall context resolve through; the Phase 4 remember-check covers it.
- **The subscribe flag.** The QA web client passes `loom: true`; a store mobile app pointed at the QA instance must show threads without errors — that is the mobile check for pull 9.
- **The name sweep** must have run before QA, so that imported live orchestrators (whose system prompts were composed with bare names) are re-launched with the new addendum on their first continuation; their in-transcript bare names are history and harmless.
- **Settings** the QA instance needs on: `continueThreadsAfterServerUpdate` (Phase 2 default), `autoResumeLimitedThreads` (3c default), the quiescence grace defaults.

<Callout tone="risk">
**Risks.** (1) *The driver work item.* If it slips, 3c-0 absorbs it and 3a's composer lands behind a default layer; the smoke cannot run until both exist. (2) *Three parties in one pi process.* Upstream's bridge, Loom's extension and the composer's argv must agree on names and ordering; the prompt-debug sidecar is the instrument — read it in every smoke run. (3) *A receipted deferral is a dead wake.* 3b's `controlMessage()` is the only place that builds a control dispatch; a coder who dispatches a `server:` id elsewhere with any mode other than the tier table's has reintroduced the strategy's risk 7. (4) *Two resume mechanisms.* Upstream's limit recovery and Loom's reroute sweep are disjoint by condition (reset time known and no fallback → upstream; otherwise Loom); the `RerouteSweep` test asserts a thread upstream will resume is left alone. (5) *The withhold is call-time.* Upstream's tools are listed; if Loom's profile fails to apply, the model sees `delegate_task` — the denial still holds, but the prompt is noisy. The profile fetch failure notifies, and the smoke's step 13 proves the denial. (6) *Mobile.* The store app decodes a closed union; the flag is the only guard — a reviewer should refuse any Loom shell-stream member sent without it. (7) *Upstream churn in `Orchestrator.ts`.* Phase 3 adds one hunk there; keep it that way.
</Callout>

# Phase 3 tracks plan — written, linted, signed, committed

**Plan:** `/home/Carl/.t3/cockpit/worktrees/loom/t3code-87358b97/plans/upstream-pull9-phase3-tracks/plan.mdx` — commit `1db85e4aea` on `t3code/plan-next-upstream-merge` (plan only staged, `--no-verify`). `lint-plan.mjs` clean (3 callouts, 7 tables, 4 mermaid, 4 file trees, annotated code, 4 checklists, question form). Signed with `sign_document` role `plan`. My branch task is ticked.

## What it delivers

One document: a **front section that is the integration contract** (19 seams: owner, shape, who lands first, what the other side stubs), the strategy's **smoke scenario made executable** (sequence diagram + 23 steps with the control-plane action and the board/thread observable each must show), then **four track sections** each with a file tree, signatures/shapes, upstream hunks, tests on V2's real orchestrator/testkit, a definition of done and a work breakdown into coder sessions with handoff points — plus hunk-inventory amendments, a 22-entry decision log, Phase 4 obligations, risks and a 3-question open form. Upstream verified at `1604ccc9d7` (one mobile commit past Phase 2's citation; all Phase 2 line refs stand).

## The seams, in brief
1. Handlers → `LoomStoreV2` + Loom commands (Phase 2 first). 2. `workstream` capability; registry issues exactly the requested set; `prepareMcp` passes `["workstream","pull-requests"]` (3a). 3. Loom pi extension assembled from **parts** — 3a owns assembler + profile/enable_toolset/ask parts, 3c adds search-guard + prompt-debug parts. 4. `LoomSessionComposer.compose(threadId)` (3a) called by the driver item's open-session hook. 5. `GET /loom/agent/session-profile` (3a) — the only per-thread carrier for the tool profile, `humanEngaged`, deny-list, prompt-debug path. 6. Control-message ids/tiers/`controlPayload.kind` enum fixed (3b → 3d renders). 7. Report file module + synthesised-report naming `<id>.quiescent-<runId>.md`. 9–10. Attention/advisories → web; liveness persists nothing. 11. Usage: `costUsd` (driver item) → `loom_usage_ledger` 1049 + `threadSpend/topSpend` (3c) → RPC+UI (3d). 12. `loom_thread_reroute` 1050 (3c). 13. PR toolkit: family + roles (3a); holds survive watch wakes by D19; 3b tests both port items. 14. **Phase 2 rule-4 refinement**: human = `createdBy user && creationSource !== "server"` (so upstream's `limit-resume`/restart "user" messages don't erase holds). 15. **`loom?: boolean` on `subscribeShell`** — goal items only to clients that ask; the store mobile app never does. 16. Dev seed (3d). 17. Migration numbers fixed. 19. One layer line per track in `loom/serverLayers.ts`.

## Most consequential choices
- **Hand-registered MCP tools** (`McpServer.addTool`, text content + `isError`), not `McpServer.toolkit` — the toolkit path JSON-stringifies results; Loom's prose rides `_meta["loom/promptSnippet"|"loom/promptGuidelines"]` and the bridge hunk reads it. Two REST routes survive (`session-profile`, `ask`/`wait`); everything else is MCP.
- **Profile re-asserted on every `before_agent_start`** (profile ∪ enabled families) — closes the bridge-retry ordering hazard; deny-list stays as second line. The human-engaged cue is `ask_user_question` becoming active (no system-prompt injection → cache prefix intact).
- **Park-and-resume rides upstream's `UsageLimitRecoveryWorker`**: the adapter hunk classifies pi quota errors as `usage_limit` with `resetAt` from Loom's health registry; Loom defaults `autoResumeLimitedThreads: true`. Loom's `RerouteSweep` keeps only what upstream can't: cross-vendor reroute (`thread.model-selection.set` + `provider-session.detach` + Loom resume; sanitiser runs pre-`switch_session`), move-back, no-reset-time resume.
- **Stuck-launch: verify-then-delete** (expected: V2's attempt/effect retry recovers both modes); if not, one liveness rule, never a CAS command. **No heartbeat table** (in-memory, floored at start). Stall suppression keys on an in-flight tool item; heartbeat advances on `turn-item.updated` — a sleeping-but-printing tool never stalls.
- **Turn baseline** = Loom reactor capturing a ref at run start + one `CheckpointCaptureService` hunk (V2's previous-checkpoint baseline includes sibling edits in a shared checkout).
- **Prose authored by a planner-preset session (3a-T)**; coders review for schema fit only.

## Decision log (abridged)
P3-1 hand registration · P3-2 `_meta` carrier · P3-3 two REST survivors · P3-4 per-turn profile re-assert · P3-5 cue = tool presence · P3-6 capability issue · P3-7 planner-authored prose · P3-8 no heartbeat table · P3-9 in-flight-tool suppression · P3-10 stuck-launch verify-then-delete · P3-11 upstream limit recovery + Loom reroute only · P3-12 reroute via model-selection.set + detach · P3-13 rule-4 refinement · P3-14 `loom` subscribe flag · P3-15 `goal_handoff` in 3a via `ThreadLaunchService.launch` · P3-16 emergent goal as reactor with deterministic id (no outbox hunk) · P3-17 turn baseline · P3-18 semantic search deferred · P3-19 drop pending-question badge, worktrees panel, relay metadata · P3-20 migration numbers · P3-21 Phase 3 adds exactly one `Orchestrator.ts` hunk (the deferred `respond` case) · P3-22 digest excerpt 400 chars.

## Things I could not settle / the parent must act on
1. **The Phase 2 driver work item** (open-session field, bundled pi, `costUsd`, patch 0001 → `switch_session`, pi 1.0.2) is assumed to exist; I could find no plan for it. The plan carries **3c-0 (conditional)** to absorb it and a default composer layer so 3a isn't blocked — but someone must confirm whether that item is planned or 3c owns it.
2. **Brief vs authority on tiers:** the brief said "gate legs and dependency kickoff via `start_if_idle`"; the strategy and Phase 2 put those in the steered tier (`queue_after_active`, converted to steer) with `start_if_idle` FYI-only. I followed the strategy/Phase 2 and said so in 3b (equivalent for kickoffs; gate legs are nested in the gate commands).
3. **Open form (3 questions):** defer semantic thread search to after cut-over (recommended); build with the staging hold present pending Carl's strategy answer (recommended); pi-intercom/unsolicited-run opt-out via per-instance env (recommended) vs uninstall.
4. The plan assumes the strategy's recommended answer on isolation (shared only, nothing ported); if Carl chooses the opt-in, it is a separate track, not a 3b change.

Ready for the gated reviewer.

sections.addendum:
<addendum>
You operate inside T3 Code's work model: Goals → Tasks → Workstream. This is how every thread here is organised, whatever its role.

A GOAL is a single durable objective that outlives any one session and spans many — the north star for all work under it. Orient to it; if work drifts from the goal, refocus or update it. A goal is decomposed into a TASK TREE: the living, shared record of what is done and what remains — for the agents working it and for the human who glances at it to re-orient. It is kept current as work progresses.

Work happens in a WORKSTREAM: a tree of durable threads. You are one thread in it, and your role overlay says how you act within it. A ROOT thread ORCHESTRATES — it plans, delegates, and reviews rather than doing the work by hand. A CHILD thread EXECUTES a single self-contained brief and hands a result back. A child is a real, persistent thread a human can open and talk to, not a throwaway: spawning one is deliberate, and a child starts fresh — it inherits none of the parent's conversation, only the brief it is given. Work flows down as briefs and back up as reports. The workstream is a graph of threads: dependencies are its edges, so dependent work waits while independent branches run in parallel (with bounded review-gate loops as the one deliberate cycle) — and the graph is not fixed; it is expected to be amended and replanned as understanding improves.

Getting information from another thread, cheapest first: a thread's REPORT is its curated hand-back — read that first. The workstream GRAPH lets you see every thread and find any of them without searching (`workstream_list`). To resolve an ambiguity, CONSULT the thread that holds the context. The full thread history can be accessed via the Pi session jsonl file if necessary.

A few principles keep this coherent:
- Your assignment is your task. For a child that is its spawn brief; at the root it is the user's direction. An inherited goal is background - align to it, but where it and your assignment differ, follow the assignment.
- Work at your level, and keep heavy sub-phases out of your context. If you orchestrate, delegate substantial work to children rather than absorbing it inline, and when new non-trivial work crystallises mid-conversation, pause to lay out or amend the graph before diving in. If you execute a brief, do it yourself rather than re-delegating it — but any thread, at any depth, may hand a bounded sub-phase of its own brief to a child when all three hold: the sub-phase is context-heavy; a short brief can carry everything it needs from you; and what comes back is an artefact — files on disk plus a short report — not understanding you must carry into later turns. Typical cases: a screenshot-capture pass, a large-corpus read, a bulk extraction. Done in situ, every page of that stays in your context for the rest of the thread; done by a child, it dies with the child. It is a trade, not a reflex: a child starts cold, so you pay to write the brief and to wait for it — a sub-phase of a few turns is cheaper inline. Where the delegation tools are dormant for your role, `enable_toolset` activates them.
- Status describes the plan; runtime is the truth. A thread's status is where it sits in the workflow; whether its agent is actually working is a separate, system-tracked fact. Lean on the system's signals for a child's state rather than inferring from a single quiet look — and if a signal looks wrong for what you can plainly see, verify rather than act blindly.
- System notices are not the human. Automated workstream notices (a child finished, needs attention, recovered) are control-plane signals for you to act on, not messages from the user.
- Your worktree is your workspace. Every edit and commit you make lands in your own worktree (your process cwd) and nowhere else — any other checkout of this project (another thread's worktree, the parent's worktree, or the project's base workspace root) is read-only context (reports, evidence), never somewhere to `cd` into and write. This matters doubly if you orchestrate: children's worktrees are cut from YOUR branch, so a file committed anywhere else — however canonical its path looks — is invisible to every child you spawn. If a brief seems to require editing outside your own worktree, that is a brief error: surface it rather than comply.
- File references in replies and reports: use the full absolute path in inline code, one span per file or directory. Do not use bare basenames, paths relative to a shell `cd`, or fenced blocks for these references. The client resolves relative paths from the thread's worktree root, not the cwd inside a bash command.
- Search your worktree, not the roots above it. Your worktree is small, but the workspace and cockpit roots that contain it are vast (every sibling worktree's node_modules), so an unbounded `find`/`grep` from one of those roots can crawl for many minutes. Never search them unscoped: stay within your worktree, or bound the walk (`-maxdepth`, a named subtree, or a tool like `rg` that skips gitignored trees) rather than let a search wander into other threads' trees. A guard blocks unbounded recursive searches outside your worktree and auto-bounds unbounded search pipelines to 30s — when a file is not where you expected, do not search wider: verify the exact paths your brief gave you first (brief paths are authoritative), then run a focused bounded search, and only as a last resort consult the thread that holds the context (`consult_thread` — expensive).
- Setup may still be running. Worktree environment setup can run in the background after you start, so before any command that needs the project environment (installs, builds, tests, typecheck, dev servers) check the setup breadcrumb — `cat "$(git rev-parse --git-dir)/t3code-setup-state.json"`: `ready` proceed; `pending` do reading/editing/planning first and re-check (poll, don't run installs yourself); `failed` inspect its `detail` and the setup terminal output, then fix or report the setup failure rather than blindly rerunning installs; file absent means no setup script was configured — assume the repo is in its normal provided state.

You are thread `0ae40d78-3680-4a90-8e3b-cf561b096e66` in this workstream: the id every workstream tool takes, the id the human sees, and the id you quote when reporting. Your own conversation history is the pi session jsonl at `$PI_SESSION_FILE` (set in every shell command you run), a file named `*_0ae40d78-3680-4a90-8e3b-cf561b096e66.jsonl`. To reach ANOTHER thread's history, use its report or `consult_thread`; its jsonl is not necessarily in the same directory as yours.

You are a planner sub-thread. Produce intent briefs and implementation plans — the thinking, not the code.

- Your spawn brief defines your assignment — the plan you owe, not a script. If you discover the brief rests on a wrong assumption, or planning surfaces something material it didn't anticipate, surface it (in the plan's risks, or via `needs_guidance` if it invalidates the brief) rather than silently re-scoping.
- Your deliverable is a plan, not an implementation. Investigate the codebase as deeply as needed, but do not write feature code — decisions and their rationale are what you hand back.
- Author plans as annotatable MDX documents per the mdx-visual-plan skill (`plans/<slug>/plan.mdx`), so the human can review and annotate them in-app before any code is written.
- A good plan states intent, decomposition into work items, contracts and risks, and acceptance criteria — enough that its correctness can be judged before implementation.
- Write for a reader with none of your context. The coder threads that implement the plan inherit nothing you've read or reasoned through; the plan must stand alone.
- Never use internal ids ('D1', 'must-fix #2') as decision titles or QuestionForm labels; name the decision and each option's outcome so they stand alone.
- Keep the task tree honest. If you are anchored, that branch is yours: tick your own tasks with `goal_task_update` the moment they land, and reshape it in ONE `goal_tasks_rewrite` if its shape stops matching the work. Tasks outside your branch are read-only — say what needs doing there in your report. Record actionable work your planning surfaces with `goal_task_add` under the phase it belongs to. Your plan's decomposition is not yours to impose on the rest of the tree: hand that intended shape back in your report, along with details, findings and verdicts.
- If your scope has sharpened beyond your spawn title, you may rename yourself with `set_thread_title` (it only ever renames the calling thread) to keep the sidebar legible.
- Your `workstream_submit` report leads with the plan's location and its key decisions. When implementation must not start until a human has approved the plan, raise `awaiting_acceptance` via `workstream_request_attention` **instead of completing** — the raise is what holds the plan, and completing in the same turn releases the coders the approval was meant to gate. Raise it only when work genuinely must wait; a plan no human has to see first just completes.

SHIPPING POLICY: merge authority is AGENT-OK — once the work is approved and required checks pass, an agent may land it on the main branch, but only by merging a PR from a feature branch via the repo's guarded ship procedure (the ship skill / `pnpm ship` where present). Never push directly to the main branch and never merge by hand; then clean up the branch.

Background context — your parent orchestrator is working toward this overall goal `ea6cb872-9915-41fc-9bed-921a93cc1d2c` (plan-next-upstream-t3-code-merge-into-loom): Pull 9 strategy: Orchestration V2 alignment
Parent's objective (background only, NOT your task): Begin working out how to proceed with the next upstream pingdotgg/t3code merge into the Loom fork, which is expected to be much more complex due to substantial upstream orchestration rewrites and new native Pi support that overlaps heavily with Loom.

What follows is a spawn snapshot of the branch you own; `goal_task_list` reads it live.

  Phase 3 — Loom's layer re-expressed on V2 in four tracks: tools, control plane, driver economics, web (01f69ecf-18c7-4dcd-a18c-194757f062d0)

Your branch — its root line is your anchor, and this block is the complete source a branch rewrite takes:
- [x] Write and review the Phase 3 track plans and the integration seams between them (d2e03942-f9ee-4665-99f5-2b2ef7651aa6)

Goal pulse: 17/47 done · 30 open tasks · 30 open outside your branch — `goal_task_list` with scope "tree" reads all of it.

Tick your own tasks with `goal_task_update` as each lands, and reshape your branch in ONE `goal_tasks_rewrite` when its shape stops matching the work: submit exactly the branch block above, keeping every retained `(id)`; your anchor stays its root line. Tasks outside your branch are read-only — record discovered work with `goal_task_add` (it lands in your branch by default; pass a parentTaskId to place it elsewhere, and the echo shows where it landed) and say what needs doing in your report. Anything you write is a short plain-language work item naming the outcome and value, for a reader outside this thread (the server rejects text over 300 characters); details, findings and verdicts go in your report or memo.

# Phase 3 tracks plan (`1db85e4aea`): review verdict is needs rework

The plan's structure works. The 19-seam front section, the per-track file trees, the decision log and the smoke table are the right shape for four parallel coders, and `lint-plan.mjs` passes. Several of its heaviest upstream claims hold at `upstream/main` `1604ccc9d7`. But checking it against source turned up 13 must-fix problems:

- It contradicts three of the orchestrator's rulings.
- Four seams don't meet: goals, notify origin, contract deltas, and wake episode keys.
- Two hold or no-silent-halt guarantees break once 3c turns `autoResumeLimitedThreads` on.
- The turn-baseline mechanism is aimed at a file that computes no diff.
- Four smoke steps can't be run as written.

All are fixable in the plan itself; none reopens the strategy.

## Verified true (no change needed)

- **P3-1.** `McpServer.toolkit` JSON-stringifies every success (`effect/dist/unstable/ai/McpServer.js:1131–1170`), and upstream itself hand-registers its image tools for this reason (`apps/server/src/mcp/McpHttpServer.ts:550–585`).
- **P3-2.** `McpSchema.Tool` has `_meta` and `addTool` keeps it. The bridge reads only name, description and inputSchema (`piT3McpExtensionSource.ts:270–300`), so the hunk that reads `_meta` works.
- **P3-4.** Pi's docs support changing selected tools in `before_agent_start`. Returning `isError: true` marks a failed call.
- **P3-9.** `tool_execution_update` → `turn_item.updated` (`PiAdapterV2.ts:1630–1635`) → `turn-item.updated` domain event (`ProviderEventIngestor.ts:463`).
- **P3-11.** `limitRecoveryCommand` honours `class: usage_limit` with `resetAt` (`UsageLimitRecoveryWorker.ts:11–71`). Its resume message is `createdBy: "user", creationSource: "server"`.
- **P3-12.** `thread.model-selection.set` and `provider-session.detach` are legal. Re-registering runs `switch_session` in a fresh process (`PiAdapterV2.ts:2016–2025`), so the sanitiser can run before it.
- **P3-17 premise.** V2's start-of-run baseline reuses the previous run's checkpoint when it exists (`RunExecutionService.ts:839`).
- **Seam 15.** `OrchestrationV2SubscribeShellInput` keys are all optional (`orchestrationV2.ts:3058–3070`). An absent flag simply means no goal items.
- **Seam 13.** The PR toolkit has exactly 5 tools.
- **Ruling 2 (wake tiers)** is applied consistently: gate legs nested, kickoff/yield/attention steered, PR-watch queued, `start_if_idle` FYI-only.

## Must-fix

**MF1 — The three rulings are not applied.**
- (a) The driver-item callout says "if that plan does not exist … 3c absorbs". Rewrite it: 3c-0 does not trigger. Mark the 3c-0 row "not triggered — owned by the Phase 2 orchestrator's driver item".
- (b) The open form still asks all three questions. Close them as decided: semantic search deferred, `held` kept as a data field, pi-intercom opt-out via an instance environment variable. Drop "(open question)" from 3d's file tree. Delete "If Carl answers otherwise, it is a separate track" (isolation).
- (c) `workstream_release` and `staged` must not be exposed:
  - delete `handlers/release.ts`;
  - change "22 defs" to 21 throughout (tests, definition of done);
  - remove `staged` from the spawn/scaffold schemas;
  - 3a-T deletes the release/staging text from roles rather than prefixing it.
- (d) `held` stays for staging. V1's `GoalHandoffHttp.ts:293–305` and `ThreadForkHttp.ts:81–109` create held roots. Specify that `goal_continue` (spawn with `held: true`) and `thread_fork` (`thread.fork` → `goal.set` → `held.set true`) stage their threads. Keep the Staged cards and the held board column unconditionally, removing "deleted if Carl retires it".

**MF2 — The driver-item boundary doesn't match Phase 2 §3.**
- Phase 2 §3 says the driver item owns the hook *that fills the field* from three `LoomStoreV2` reads, plus the launch-identity sidecar. The Phase 3 plan instead moves composition into 3a's `LoomSessionComposer`, and lists `launchIdentity.ts` under 3a as a bare file move. No one specifies writing the launch identity at launch or replaying argv for a `forkFrom` child.
- "What the tracks start from" omits the sidecar.
- Fix: state explicitly that Phase 3 narrows Phase 2 §3 (the hook is a one-line call to `compose(threadId)` with a default layer), and name one owner and a shape for identity capture and replay. I added a Phase 2 task so the parent can pass this to the driver-item planner.

**MF3 — The pending-steer stash is orphaned.**
- Phase 2's recovery table says "the steer stash rides it — driver item". Ruling 1's list of driver-item deliverables excludes it, and Phase 3 has no stash anywhere. Detach-ledger row DT-24 tags it "3b, 2".
- Smoke step 17 asserts "C resumes with its pending steer delivered", so nothing would build what the gate checks.
- Fix: assign `pendingSteering.ts` to 3b or 3c, with a file-tree row, the seam it feeds and a test.

**MF4 — One human predicate, applied everywhere; the current mix causes a silent halt.**
- Seam 14 refines rule 4 to `createdBy user && creationSource !== "server"`. That is stricter, so it does not bring back hold erasure. But two readers still treat upstream's limit-resume (`createdBy: "user"`) as human:
  - P3-5's `humanEngaged` reads `latestUserAuthoredMessageAt`, which counts any `createdBy = 'user'` message (`ProjectionStore.ts:4910–4918`, `:1403`);
  - Phase 2's `quiescenceCandidate` sets `humanStarted = createdBy === "user"`.
- With 3c defaulting `autoResumeLimitedThreads` to true, every child that is resumed after a quota event gets `ask_user_question` (contradicting "children consult their parent"). And because the human grace is null, it never goes quiescent: if it ends its turn without submitting, it sits in progress with no flag. That is a silent halt.
- Phase 2's `startNextQueuedRun` hunk (in `Orchestrator.ts`) also has its own unrefined `createdBy: "user"` test.
- Fix: one exported `isHumanAuthored(message)` in `Orchestrator.loom.ts`, used by rule 4, the `startNextQueuedRun` hunk, quiescence's `humanStarted`, and the profile's `humanEngaged` (computed from messages, not the shell field). Consider keying on `usageLimitContinuationOfRunId === undefined` instead of `creationSource`. The fall-through answer of `runtime-request.respond` is a genuine human answer but is `createdBy user / creationSource server` (`Orchestrator.ts:7006–7016`).

**MF5 — Upstream's limit-resume ignores Loom state.**
- `limitRecoveryCommand` doesn't check outcome, attention or held. V1's `ExhaustionResumeSweep.ts:241–247` skipped done and cancelled threads. Under this plan, a child that hits its quota and is then cancelled, or set done, or flagged `needs_guidance`, resumes at `resetAt` with "Continue where you left off" and edits the shared checkout.
- Fix: extend Phase 2's rule-0 veto in `loomTurnStartRules` (a Loom file) to `usageLimitContinuationOfRunId`, using the same not-continued set as restart continuation. Add a 3c test.

**MF6 — Goals never reach the web client.**
- client-runtime loads the authoritative snapshot over HTTP (`/api/orchestration/shell`, served by `orchestration-v2/http.ts:95–108`), then subscribes with `afterSequence` (`client-runtime/state/shell.ts:244–284`). That resume path sends a project-metadata snapshot with `threads: []` (`ws.ts:1126–1145`). Phase 2 put goals only on the ws `loadSnapshot`.
- Fix (3d, add to the hunk inventory):
  - add `goals` to the http.ts snapshot. Unflagged is fine, since the store app strips the extra key;
  - on a `loom: true` resumed subscription, emit the current goals as `goal.updated` items before live;
  - the reducer must not clear goals on a resume snapshot that lacks them.

**MF7 — `notify_thread` (3a-3) and notify delivery (3b) via `sendToThread` lose `loom.origin`.**
- `ThreadManagementSendInput` has no `loom` field, and the dispatch it builds omits it (`ThreadManagementService.ts:101–114`, `:568–582`). Phase 2's dispatch table specifies `message.dispatch` with `deliveryIntent: "auto"` and `loom.origin`.
- Fix: dispatch `message.dispatch` directly with `deliveryIntent: "auto"`, `senderThreadId` and `loom: { origin }` for notify. State the same explicitly for `workstream_prompt`, because rule 4's "parent clears the hold" depends on `origin: orchestrator`.

**MF8 — Wake episode keys don't match stored state.**
- The yield id uses `<outcomeEventId>`, but a yield never writes `outcome-set`, so that field is null or stale. A second yield episode would collide with the first one's receipt and never be delivered. V1 keyed on the outcome-recorded event id (`WorkstreamDispatcher.ts:815–824`). Use `lastOutcome.eventId`.
- The attention id uses `<attentionEventId>`, which nothing in the sidecar stores. Specify where it comes from (a stored id per reason, or an event-store read).

**MF9 — The contract deltas Phase 3 needs have no owner.**
- Phase 2 carries V1's `ControlPayload.kind = ["digest","yield","notice"]` unchanged (`orchestration.loom.ts:723–731`). Seam 6 fixes 12 kinds and item flags; "advisory (spinning, slow-tool, recovered)" and `quiescent` versus `yield`+`synthesised` are ambiguous.
- Seam 8 needs `lastOutcome.synthesised`, which `WorkOutcomeRecord` lacks.
- `runtime-request.create` needs a new command member and a Loom marker on `OrchestrationV2RuntimeRequest`, which has no metadata slot and requires a `nodeId` (`orchestrationV2.ts:968–987`).
- The tier table nests "gate-resolution" in the gate command, but Phase 2's `thread.gate.resolve` has no message field and targets the counterpart. Smoke steps 4–5 have the parent learn of resolution through the FYI digest instead.
- No track's file tree lists `orchestrationV2.loom.ts`, and the hunk inventory has no runtime-request row.
- Fix: one owner per delta and the exact enum. Say the resolution reaches the parent only through the digest. Specify the request's marker, `nodeId` source and `responseCapability: message`. Land the contract deltas first.

**MF10 — The turn-baseline hunk is in the wrong file, and its test can't pass.**
- `CheckpointCaptureService` has no diff base. The file summary diffs against `previousCheckpointRef` inside `CheckpointService.capture` (`CheckpointService.ts:~360–440`). The Diff panel diffs from the previous turn's checkpoint in `checkpointing/CheckpointDiffQuery.getTurnDiff` (`:158–190`).
- A reactor on `run.updated → running` races the agent's first edit. V2's own `captureBaseline` runs before the provider starts.
- `baseline.test` ("excludes a file B edited *during* A's run") is impossible with a start-of-turn baseline. V1's semantics are "sibling edits *between* this thread's turns".
- Fix: name the real hunk sites (or one hunk making `captureBaseline` write a per-run Loom ref that both diff sites prefer), and restate the test and smoke step 23.

**MF11 — `waiting = pendingRuntimeRequest.kind === "approval"` can never be true.**
- The kinds are command, file-read, file-change, mcp-elicitation, permission, dynamic_tool_call, user_input and auth_refresh (`providerPolicy.ts:38–44`, `orchestrationV2.ts:973–976`).
- Fix: map the approval kinds explicitly, both here and in seam 9's derived `awaiting_approval`.

**MF12 — The smoke can't be run as written, and misses cases the strategy names.**
- Step 16 needs a running grandchild, but none exists and X is already done.
- Steps 17 and 21 use C after it is done.
- Step 18 puts a silent tool into an in-flight-tool window, where the plan's own suppression means no nudge. Use a frozen model stream with no tool, and add the slow-tool advisory as the observable for a silent tool.
- S is never spawned (used at steps 10 and 14), and notifying an unstarted S kicks it off.
- Missing cases:
  - a coder in rework goes quiet and is yielded, not looped back to the reviewer;
  - a child that just answered a human does not go quiescent;
  - after a steered yield, the child's `awaiting_orchestrator` is still standing.

**MF13 — Detach-ledger rows owed to Phase 3 tracks are not dispositioned.**
- The plan dispositions only the web rows, plus the claim "everything else in DT-31–39 is re-attached".
- Missing or silent: DT-24 (stash), DT-26 (`t3 goal` CLI, tagged 3a), DT-36 (user-input panel hunks, 3a/I), DT-38's goal-keeping hunks (`useHandleNewThread` `goalId`, `goalDraftBucketKey`), DT-44 (emergent-goal TextGeneration op, 3b), DT-22a's `stallContext`/`threadResolve`.
- Fix: a plan-level table covering every DT row tagged 3x, each with a track and a disposition.

## Nice-to-have

1. The registration sketch should take `McpInvocationContext` from the fiber, as upstream does (`McpHttpServer.ts:411–418`).
2. The function is `prepareMcpSession`, not `prepareMcp` (`ProviderSessionManager.ts:437`).
3. Restart continuation is `createdBy: "agent"` (`RestartContinuation.ts:156–172`), not "user". Fix the text in seam 14 and P3-13.
4. 3b's trigger list drops the Phase 2 reactor's archived, unarchived, deleted and goal-set triggers, so cascades wait for the 60 s tick.
5. Migration 1049: V1's table has `event_id` as a NOT NULL primary key and differently named columns. SQLite needs a `CREATE UNIQUE INDEX` rather than an added constraint. Give the column mapping.
6. The fallback-chain settings change is a decode-time `settings.json` transform, not a 1001+ migration.
7. Name a first lander for the shared Loom-only files the plan doesn't list: `loom/wsMethods.ts`, `rpc.loom.ts`, the `contracts/rpc.ts` splice (3b and 3d), and `settings.loom.ts` (3b and 3c).
8. `goal_handoff`: when `launch(initialMessage)` runs before `goal.set`, the first session may compose without goal context. Use launch → `goal.set` → dispatch the brief.
9. The test "`set_outcome done` refused with `pendingRework`" contradicts Phase 2's arm (allowed with a warning). Say it is self-issued only.
10. Area H: `modelSelection.ts` must emit upstream's `thinking` option id. The stored-selection migration has no owner.
11. Stuck-launch verification moves from the driver item (Phase 2) to 3b. Say so.
12. The track map, P3-21 and seam 14 disagree about which `Orchestrator.ts` edits Phase 3 makes.
13. Name the steerability check behind the stall nudge's "escalate instead of queue".
14. The families test lumps HUMAN_INPUT in with the MCP defs, but `ask_user_question` is registered by the extension.

## For the parent

Pass the Phase 2 driver-item boundary (MF2 and MF3) to the Phase 2 orchestrator. It is tracked as Phase 2 task `f1ebb03e`.

Ruling 2 covers wake tiers.

This means the argv-building step in the adapter never needs to know about forking at all, since identical composer inputs guarantee identical argv — so the `forkFrom` field originally proposed for the adapter in Phase 2 becomes unnecessary there, since replay logic lives entirely in the composer.

# Round 2 delta review: Phase 3 tracks plan `63a80ca7ee`

**Verdict: one more round needed.** All 13 round-1 must-fixes are resolved and lint passes. But moving launch identity into the composer (the MF2 fix) removed the only mechanism that forked a `forkFrom` spawn child's pi session. That is one new must-fix.

## Round-1 findings: resolved

- **MF1 — rulings.** Callout rewritten; 3c-0 marked "not triggered"; the open-questions form replaced with "None"; the isolation hedge deleted. `release.ts` and `staged` are removed, and the count is 21 defs. The "Staged roots" paragraph names the two writers of `held` (goal_continue, thread_fork). The staged cards and the held column are now unconditional.
- **MF2 — driver-item boundary.** The narrowing of Phase 2 §3 is stated explicitly, and composition is the composer's. This introduced the new finding below.
- **MF3 — steer stash.** Owned through seam 20: 3c writes and clears it, 3b redelivers it, and smoke step 17 asserts the redelivered text.
- **MF4 — one human predicate.** `isHumanAuthored` is keyed on `usageLimitContinuationOfRunId`. It is stamped once as `loom.humanAuthored` and read by rule 4, `startNextQueuedRun`, quiescence and `humanEngaged`. I checked this against source:
  - the respond fall-through goes through `dispatchMessage` (`Orchestrator.ts:7006–7016`), so it gets the stamp;
  - restart continuation is created by an agent (`RestartContinuation.ts:156–172`), not a user.
- **MF5 — limit-resume.** Rule 0's veto now covers usage-limit continuations, and a test asserts it.
- **MF6 — goals reach the web.** Goals are on the `orchestration-v2/http.ts` snapshot, replayed on a resumed `loom: true` subscription, and the reducer no longer clears them on a resume.
- **MF7 — notify/prompt.** Both dispatch `message.dispatch` directly, with the reason stated.
- **MF8 — episode keys.** Yields and digests key on `lastOutcome.eventId`; attention keys on `attentionEpisodes[reason]`.
- **MF9 — contract deltas.** Session 3a-0 lands them first. `ControlPayload` keeps Phase 2's three kinds; gate resolution reaches the parent only as a digest item. The `loom-ask:` id prefix marks Loom requests, and the request uses the active run's root node.
- **MF10 — turn baseline.** Moved into `CheckpointService.captureBaseline`, preferred by both diff sites. The test now uses edits made between runs.
- **MF11 — approval kinds.** Listed in all three places.
- **MF12 — smoke.** S, Y and G are spawned; step 3 has C go quiet during rework and yield; step 9 covers "answered a human, so not quiescent"; steps 17 and 21 use D; step 18 uses `kill -STOP`; step 19 adds the slow-tool line.
- **MF13 — detach ledger.** A full disposition table is in place.

All 14 round-1 nice-to-haves are applied.

## Must-fix (new, exposed by the MF2 rework)

**R2-MF1 — a `forkFrom` spawn child no longer gets its source's conversation.**

- **What the plan does now.** P3-23 removes `forkFrom` from the open-session field. The composer replays only the prompt identity (prompt, skills, extensions, model, tool profile). The plan says "the native fork itself is V2's `thread.fork`".
- **Why that isn't enough.** A `forkFrom` child is created by Phase 2's `thread.spawn`, which nests `thread.created` with `forkedFrom: null` (Phase 2 D7), never `thread.fork`. Only `thread_fork` uses `thread.fork`. The strategy's Area L assumed upstream's fork plus Loom's identity replay; the open-session `forkFrom` member was where the driver forked the session.
- **Consequence.** As written, a `forkFrom` child opens a fresh pi session. It has a byte-identical system prompt but none of the source's transcript, so acknowledge-then-fork silently loses its whole point. Nothing errors.
- **Correction — pick one and say who builds it:**
  - (a) Keep a `forkFrom: { sourceThreadId }` member on the open-session field, used only for the native session fork (driver item). The composer still owns prompt identity. Tell the parent this reverses half of boundary change (1).
  - (b) Have the spawn handler or arm create a `forkFrom` child through V2's fork path (a pending `native_fork` context transfer on the child), keeping `subagent` lineage. Say how that coexists with D7's `forkedFrom: null`.
- **Test.** Add one: the first run of a `forkFrom` child sees the source's history.

## Nice-to-have

1. Line 195 still says "applies it to all 22"; it should be 21.
2. Line 218 still says "the staging vocabulary is removed if Carl retires the hold". Per the ruling: staging vocabulary for spawn/scaffold is deleted; staged-root wording stays.
3. Seam 20 redelivers stashed steers after upstream's continuation even for threads in rule 0's not-continued set (flagged, cancelled). A control message would then start a turn on a held thread. Skip redelivery for that set and leave the stash for the human's first message.
4. Phase 4 obligations: imported messages carry no `loom.humanAuthored`. Either the importer stamps V1 human-origin user messages, or imported human-engaged roots read as not engaged.
5. Smoke sequencing: step 16 cancels G before step 19 observes it. Note that step 19's observation happens before step 16.
